readerTitle: Brands you recognize without the logo
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Tiffany & Co., Coca-Cola) + 실제 연구 (Romaniuk의 독특한 브랜드 자산 연구) + 가상 적용 (지역 할인마트, 국수 체인)
insight: 브랜드 자산의 역할은 무언가를 '뜻하는' 것이 아니라 '우리 것'으로 바로 알아보게 하는 것이다. 그래서 많이 알려져 있고(유명성) 경쟁사와 겹치지 않는지(고유성)로 판단한다.
misconception: 색, 모양, 캐릭터는 제품의 장점을 표현해야 하고, 오래되면 새롭게 바꿔야 효과가 있다.

sources.text: Romaniuk, J. (2018). Building Distinctive Brand Assets. Oxford University Press.
Tiffany & Co., company history (Blue Book catalogue, Tiffany Blue box, Pantone 1837 Blue)
The Coca-Cola Company, history of the contour bottle (1915 design)

factChecks.note: Tiffany Blue: 1845년 Blue Book 카탈로그 표지에 처음 쓰였다는 내용과 Pantone이 창립 연도를 딴 '1837 Blue'로 표준화했다는 내용을 Tiffany 공식 자료로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도를 'since the 1800s' 수준으로만 적었습니다.
Coca-Cola 컨투어 병: 1915년 디자인 공모에서 '어둠 속에서 만져도, 깨진 조각만 봐도 알아볼 수 있는 병'을 요구했다는 이야기는 회사 자료에 나오지만 표현이 자료마다 다릅니다. 카드에 'reportedly'로 표시했습니다.
Romaniuk의 두 기준(fame: 카테고리 구매자 중 이 자산을 브랜드와 연결하는 비율, uniqueness: 경쟁 브랜드와 연결하지 않는 정도)을 원서로 확인하세요. 카드에는 쉬운 말로 풀었습니다.
할인마트와 국수 체인 사례는 설명용 가상 사례이며 수치를 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: A small blue box with no name on it
body: Picture a robin's-egg blue box tied with a white ribbon. No logo in sight.
Many people can still tell you which jeweler it came from. That color is doing a job most logos can't.

image.label: A plain light-blue gift box with a white ribbon
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 밝은 청록빛(로빈 에그 블루) 선물 상자에 흰 리본. 로고·글자·상표는 전혀 넣지 않음. 부드러운 조명, 상자만 중앙에.

cards.title: The agency says your fox looks dated.
body: You run a regional chain of discount grocery stores. For 15 years your bags, signs and flyers have used bright orange and a hand-drawn fox.
A new agency proposes a sleek navy look. Shoppers say they spot your orange bags across a parking lot. What do you do?

options.text: Switch to the navy look to feel more modern
options.feedback: You gain a fresher style but throw away 15 years of shoppers linking orange and the fox to you. Navy has to be learned from zero.

options.text: Keep the orange and the fox, and modernize everything around them
options.feedback: You refresh the look while keeping the cues people already recognize. This is the idea in this lesson.

options.text: Keep the fox but move it onto navy
options.feedback: You save one cue but drop the one people notice from a distance. Half the memory goes with the color.

cards.title: Tiffany made a color mean one store.
body: Tiffany & Co. has used its light blue since the 1800s, first on its catalogue and then on its boxes and bags. It never swapped it for a trendier shade.
Over time the color itself became a signal. A blue box in a hand or a photo tells people which store it came from before anyone reads a word.
The company even worked with Pantone to standardize the exact shade, so it looks the same everywhere.

cards.title: Distinctive assets
body: **Distinctive assets** are the colors, shapes, characters, sounds or phrases that make people think of your brand, even without your name.
Researcher Jenni Romaniuk suggests two tests. **Fame:** do most buyers in your market link this cue to you? **Uniqueness:** do they link it to you and not to rivals?
A cue that passes both can stand in for your logo.

image.label: A 2x2 grid: famous vs unknown, unique vs shared
image.brief: 2x2 매트릭스 인포그래픽. 가로축 "Shared with rivals → Unique to you", 세로축 "Few know it → Most know it". 오른쪽 위 칸만 강조 색으로 "Use it everywhere". 다른 칸: "Avoid", "Build it", "Category cue". 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: Built to be known in a glance.
body: In 1915, Coca-Cola asked designers for a bottle people could reportedly recognize in the dark, or even when broken. The curved contour bottle was the result.
Buyers rarely study brands. They glance. Distinctive assets help in two moments:
list: **At the shelf:** people find you fast among look-alikes
**In ads and on the street:** people credit the right brand, not a rival
cards.softwareNote: In software, assets include an app icon's shape and color, a notification sound or a mascot. On a crowded phone screen, a familiar icon is found faster than a name is read.

cards.title: It doesn't need to mean anything.
body: Blue says nothing about jewelry. An orange fox says nothing about groceries. What matters is the link in buyers' memories, not the meaning.

The opposite trap is the **category cue**. Green leaves on organic food or a steaming cup on a café sign tell people what kind of business you are. Rivals use them too, so they don't tell people it's you.

cards.title: Slow to build, quick to lose.
body: An asset only works after years of steady use. A new color or mascot is just decoration until enough people link it to you.
So don't drop your name too early, and don't bet everything on a cue nobody knows yet. Ask a few customers what it reminds them of before you treat it as an asset.
And when you redesign, list your assets first. Losing one can cost far more than the new look gains.

cards.title: Now it's a noodle chain.
body: You run 12 noodle restaurants and want people to spot your brand on signs, takeaway bags and ads. Which should you build on?

options.text: A red bowl with an unusual notched rim, used on every sign, bag and ad
options.feedback: It is unique and repeatable everywhere. It takes time to become famous, but it can become yours alone.

options.text: A bowl with steam and chopsticks
options.feedback: It says 'noodles' clearly, but so does every rival's sign. It helps the category, not you.

options.text: A catchy new slogan for each season's campaign
options.feedback: Slogans can become assets, but only if you keep one for years. Changing it each season resets the memory.

cards.title: Own a few cues people link only to you.
body: A distinctive asset is valuable when many buyers know it and link it to you alone. Pick a few, use them everywhere, and keep them.
**Try it today:** cover your name on your sign or package. Ask three customers who it belongs to. What did they recognize?
